questions.q: What is the "grain" of a fact table?
options: A one-sentence statement of exactly what a single row in the fact table represents
The physical storage format of the table on disk
The number of columns the table contains
The name of the primary key column
questions.explain: Grain is a precise statement of meaning — for example, "one row per order line" — not a technical detail about columns or storage.

questions.q: Why does grain have to be declared before choosing dimensions or facts?
options: SQL Server requires grain to be declared in a system table first
Dimensions must always be chosen before any grain statement exists
Every dimension key and measure a fact table can legitimately hold is determined by its grain
Grain has no real effect on which columns belong in the table
questions.explain: A column only belongs in a fact table if it's meaningful at that table's grain — for example, ProductKey only fits an order-line grain, not an order-level grain.

questions.q: What does Kimball recommend regarding atomic vs. summarized grain?
options: Build the atomic (lowest-detail) grain first, and add summarized/aggregate tables on top of it for performance later
Atomic grain should never be used in a data warehouse
Grain choice makes no difference to what questions can later be answered
Always build only summarized grain to save storage
questions.explain: Atomic-grain data can answer questions not yet anticipated; summarized data is locked to the level it was rolled up to. Aggregates belong on top of atomic data, not instead of it.

questions.q: What is the single most common fact-table design mistake related to grain?
options: Choosing a grain that is too atomic
Mixing two different grains in one table, distinguished only by which columns happen to be populated
Storing the grain statement as a comment in the CREATE TABLE script
Using too many surrogate keys in the same table
questions.explain: A table that silently holds rows at two grains breaks additivity — summing measures across rows now double-counts or under-counts, since not every row represents the same thing.

questions.q: A fact table's grain statement describes it as "one row per order, or one row per order line." What does the word "or" signal here?
options: It means the table is automatically a snowflake schema
This is a perfectly valid, well-designed grain statement
This is actually a warning sign of two fact tables mixed into one, and it needs to be split before adding columns
It means the table has no grain at all
questions.explain: A grain statement that needs "and" or "or" to describe it is describing two different fact tables, not one — a clear signal to split the design before proceeding.
